Many thought AI would make senior developers less needed.
But it turned out: the more code AI writes, the more you need someone who knows what to do with that code.
AI really did make development faster.
But along with speed, the number of decisions you have to check grew too.
AI can suggest an architecture, write a service, build an API, generate SQL and tests.
But someone has to understand whether that solution really fits this exact project.
That's where experience shows.
An experienced engineer looks beyond whether the code works right now.
He asks questions:
What happens when the load grows?
What if an external service goes down?
How will this be maintained in six months?
What about the data?
So after AI, software engineering didn't become less important.
What changed is where the engineer is needed.
If you're a developer and use AI a lot, I wouldn't try to learn every single AI tool.
I'd strengthen the foundation:
architecture, databases,
Git, Docker, networking,
debugging, security.
AI can speed a developer up,
but only engineering thinking tells you where to point that speed.
What engineering thinking is built on, I broke down in my Telegram.
